text: Once deployed on edge devices, a deep neural network model should dynamically adapt to newly discovered environments and personalize its utility for each user. The system must be capable of continual learning, i.e., learning new information from a temporal stream of data in situ without forgetting previously acquired knowledge. However, creating a personalized continual learning framework poses significant challenges due to limited compute and storage resources on edge devices. Existing methods rely on large memory storage to preserve past data while learning from incoming streams, making them impractical for such devices. In this paper, we propose Chameleon as a hardware-friendly continual learning solution for user-centric continual learning with dual replay buffers. The strategy takes advantage of the hierarchical memory structure commonly found in edge devices, utilizing a short-term replay store in on-chip memory and a long-term replay store in off-chip memory. We also present an FPGA-based analytical model to estimate the compute and communication costs of the dual replay strategy on the hardware, making effective design choices considering various latent layer options. We conduct extensive experiments on four different models, demonstrating our method's consistent performance across diverse model architectures. Our method achieves up to 7× speedup and improved energy efficiency on popular edge devices, including ZCU102 FPGA, NVIDIA Jetson Nano, and Google's EdgeTPU. Our code is available at https://github.com/ecolab-nus/Chameleon.

Conventional machine learning (ML) algorithms demonstrate excellent performance when applied to fixed datasets with iterative gradient-based methods [2]. Such methods usually loop over the entire dataset multiple times, assuming the data remains static and accessible beforehand. However, the utilization of such multi-epoch (joint) training methods incurs substantial computational and memory costs, rendering them impractical for edge devices.

For real-time applications, edge devices should ideally learn from a small number of data instances at a time in a single pass. The tight memory constraints on most edge devices do not allow the deployed model to loop over the entire dataset for multiple epochs, as commonly done in traditional machine learning approaches. Furthermore, it is crucial for the model to efficiently acquire knowledge from the incoming data stream without gradually losing relevant past information.

Online Continual Learning (CL) (also known as lifelong learning) [4], [5] studies the problem of learning from an online non-independent and identically distributed (non-iid) data stream while dealing with the issue of catastrophic forgetting (CF) [6], i.e., forgetting old information in the presence of more recent information. Replay-based CL methods [7] are the most popular and effective at mitigating CF. They store a subset of incoming data samples in an external buffer and periodically train (replay) the network with these previously seen instances.

Figure 2 shows the memory requirements for various methods incrementally learning images from the CORe50 dataset [3]. As can be seen, naive single-epoch (finetuning) training becomes impractical in practice with ∼15% accuracy. Such a method fails to adapt to varying domains due to catastrophic forgetting. The weight update rule [8] rapidly overwrites the model parameters when learning a data distribution under domain shift, where the probability distribution of the data varies over time.

On the other hand, memory requirements for replay-based methods pose an additional burden on already constrained on-chip storage available on edge devices [9]. For instance, Google's EdgeTPU [10] has only 8 MB of on-chip SRAM. The state-of-the-art replay-based methods such as Experience Replay (ER) [11] and Dark Experience Replay (DER) [12] exhibit dismal accuracy (< 65%) under limited memory budgets. They perform better with increasing buffer sizes, but such large memory requirements become infeasible on the edge.

Moreover, the memory footprint of the model parameters and activations leaves only a fraction of on-device memory for replay. This, in turn, compels the system to store/retrieve replay samples from the off-chip DRAM. However, the offchip DRAM accesses are extremely power-hungry and incur huge latency costs, as studied in previous studies [13]. Offchip memory accesses consume approximately 120 times more power than on-chip memory accesses. Consequently, methods such as Latent Replay [14] with slightly better accuracy under limited memory budgets incur up to 7x more latency and energy when deployed on an embedded FPGA accelerator compared to our proposed method, as discussed in results. These observations naturally highlight the necessity for an optimal strategy to minimize DRAM accesses and effectively manage the replay buffer.

To tackle with these challenges, we propose Chameleon for low-latency, energy-efficient continual learning to achieve two major objectives simultaneously: (i) overcoming the daunting issue of catastrophic forgetting (ii) within the limited on-chip memory available on embedded devices. Figure 2 shows the relative advantage of Chameleon, achieving roughly 79.5% accuracy with only 0.3 MB of on-chip memory outperforming other state-of-the-art CL methods on the CORe50 dataset.

To achieve these goals, we first introduce a dual-memory replay mechanism incorporating a short-term (ST) and a longterm (LT) buffer. The novel replay framework allows us to take advantage of the memory hierarchy on most hardware, comprising a small on-chip memory with low energy cost and a large off-chip memory with very high energy cost. For this purpose, we develop two sampling strategies that carefully balance the trade-off between the uncertain and representative instances from the incoming data stream. For the short-term store, we introduce a sampling method based on user affinity and uncertainty to quickly collect the most difficult-to-learn samples, most of which belong to user-preferred classes. Finally, we propose a novel class-prototype-based sampling scheme leveraging inter-class diversity to retain the most meaningful information for the long-term store.

However, exploring different layers and understanding the accuracy-hardware trade-off for various latent layers and machine learning models can be a daunting task. To address the vast design space and various latent layer choices given a model, in this work, we propose a flexible cost-modeling framework to accurately estimate the cost of computation and data transfer, enabling us to make more informed decisions with respect to efficient hardware deployment. We choose FPGAs for this exploration due to their reconfigurability, making them an ideal platform for such exploration.

Designing continually evolving user-specific models requires on-device training on edge devices. Previous works [15], [16] primarily focused on designing efficient CNN inference accelerators on FPGAs leveraging various optimization techniques such as tiling, loop unrolling, and loop transformation. Recently, several FPGA designs [17], [18] have been proposed to accelerate large-scale training on the cloud. However, there remains a significant gap with limited exploration into FPGA-based continual learning (CL) frameworks. We present Chameleon-Accel, an FPGA-based continual learning acceleration framework to comprehensively analyze the relative advantage of Chameleon, our hierarchical replay-buffer-based technique, compared to existing works such as Latent Replay with a single replay-buffer.

The previous version of our work [19] introduces a novel, accurate, low-latency, user-preference-aware continual learning approach for resource-constrained edge devices. The approach proposes a dual-memory replay mechanism incorporating on-chip short-term and off-chip long-term buffer to overcome catastrophic forgetting with limited memory. The current version of the work expands on the previous contributions and introduces the following additional main contributions:

• We introduce Chameleon-Accel, an FPGA-based hardware acceleration framework complementing our existing user-preference aware continual learning technique. Traditional machine learning (ML) algorithms are designed to train on static datasets by making multiple passes over the entire training data. In this context, standard ML frameworks like neural networks employ iterative gradient-based methods, where small parameter updates are performed at each iteration to minimize the loss. However, when learning from data distributions that change over time in terms of their states or probability distributions, this weight update rule rapidly overwrites network parameters. As shown in Figure 3, each new data stream corresponds to a completely unique model in a conventional machine learning setup.

In contrast, continual learning (CL), also referred to as incremental or lifelong learning, aims to learn incrementally from a non-stationary data stream. CL addresses the need to learn from non-independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) data distributions in a more realistic scenario, as illustrated in Figure 3. The primary objective of CL is to mitigate catastrophic forgetting, which refers to the phenomenon where a model loses its ability to retain previously acquired knowledge while learning from recent data. To achieve this, CL frameworks simulate an infinite stream of training data, where at each time step, the model encounters new samples drawn from a non-i.i.d. data distribution and transfer knowledge when encountering a new data stream. This setup allows the model to adapt and learn from new data while preserving past information. By focusing on continual learning, our work aims to focus on techniques that enable machine learning models to learn in dynamic environments and maintain their knowledge over time. The mitigation of catastrophic forgetting and the ability to continually adapt to new data are crucial for the practical deployment of machine learning systems in realworld scenarios.

There are three primary continual learning techniques: regularization techniques, architecture-based techniques, and replay-based techniques. Regularization-based methods such as online Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC++) [20] and Learning Without Forgetting (LwF) [21] constrain weight updates, while the architecture-based techniques dynamically grow network space to preserve information corresponding to newly seen tasks. However, the majority of these existing methods are primarily designed for cloud-centered training and are not well-suited for resource-constrained edge devices.

Replay-based (also known as rehearsal) methods offer the most effective approach for continual learning on edge devices. Replay-based techniques store a representation of previously learned knowledge with the new data. Early works such as ER [11] interleave new incoming data with old, already seen data stored in a buffer to mitigate catastrophic forgetting during continual learning. GSS [22] introduces a gradient directionbased sample selection strategy to optimally select the most relevant replay instances; however, limited to simple image classification tasks such as MNIST [23] and CIFAR [24]. Several works, such as OCS [25] and Coreset [26], maintain data summaries of the incoming streaming data via small, weighted subsets of the data. While these methods provide efficient storage mechanisms, their computational demands make them infeasible for resource-constrained devices. Other works such as DER [12] and PRE-DFKD [27] leverage Knowledge Distillation [28], combining replay with the distillation loss and achieving superior performance over various other baselines. More advanced continual learning methods, such as C-FSCIL [29], propose a hyperdimensional computing based solution for class-incremental learning in a few-shot setting.

More recently, Latent Replay [14] stores feature maps from the middle (latent) layers of the network in place of raw input images via uniform random sampling. This helps them store more samples in the replay buffer within the same memory budget. Further, these approaches fix the early layers of the network since these layers are highly transferable across domains and train the other half to reduce the training cost. However, these works are agnostic of the underlying memory hierarchy of the device, consuming up to 50 MB or more of extra memory for replay. As discussed before, such a large memory requirement cannot be satisfied with limited on-chip storage on edge devices. As a result, these methods suffer from high latency and energy costs to access and retrieve samples from the off-chip memory for rehearsal.

To address this shortcoming, we build upon the concept of Latent Replay and propose a novel approach that addresses the memory constraints of edge devices. We introduce dualreplay buffers, varying in two ways: capacity and access frequency. The short-term memory is 10-15 times smaller than the long-term memory and is updated more frequently. We allow the seamless acquisition of new information by replacing short-term samples with new ones from the stream at every iteration. Likewise, as the long-term samples are used to retain cumulative information of all classes, they are updated less frequently.

In addition to replay-based techniques, recent methods such as SLDA [30] offer dynamic adaptation to varying domain shifts via an online non-parametric classifier. However, SLDA incurs high computational costs due to the pseudo-inverse matrix operation, making it unsuitable for the edge. In summary, while existing continual learning techniques have shown promise, their applicability to resource-constrained edge devices is limited. Our proposed approach aims to overcome these limitations by introducing a memory-efficient replay mechanism tailored for edge devices, enabling effective continual learning in real-world edge computing scenarios.

text: Recent works such as [31] propose Latent Replay based hardware primitives to deploy CL on a PULP platform. [32] demonstrate continual learning in a few-shot learning scenario on an in-memory compute core. Another work [33] focuses on a specialized accelerator with a selective weight update strategy and optimized dataflow techniques for activations. Despite these contributions, a comprehensive framework for continual user adaptation at the edge, integrating on-device training, continual learning, and model personalization, has been lacking. In this context, our Chameleon-Accel framework presents a novel paradigm, coalescing these essential components together to achieve continual user adaptation on edge devices. A naive machine learning algorithm would not be able to remember previously learned information without any access to old data, resulting in catastrophic forgetting. For this purpose, we adopt a replay-based strategy to maintain previously seen samples in a buffer to rehearse them with the incoming data stream. Therefore, given the data stream D, the goal of our continual learning framework is to maintain two replay buffers M s (on-chip) and M l (off-chip) such that we can maximize the accuracy corresponding to classes of interest within the memory and compute capability of the device.

As shown in Figure 4, the method consists of a DNN coupled with two-stage storage: (M s , M l ) mimicking the onchip/off-chip memory subsystem on the underlying hardware. The DNN model can be defined as g(f (•)) consisting of two nested functions: f ( • ) is fixed and extracts higherdimensional feature representations (latent activations) of the inputs while g( • ) undergoes model training and maps latent activations to their categorical classes. The two functions are parameterized by θ and ϕ, respectively. Our training algorithm performs only single step forward and backward update for each data sample, considering the resource-constrained environment.

As illustrated in Figure 4 and algorithm 1, given an incoming batch of data B t = (X t , Y t ), where the time step t tends to T , our framework processes samples in a five-step process. The first step consists of user-preference estimation 1 . We estimate user preferences on-device by tracking the frequency of samples n c (Line 3) corresponding to each class. Specifically, we identify the most frequently occurring k classes as user-preferred classes. Since our learning scenario is agnostic of the total number of samples to be seen across the stream, the tracking mechanism re-calibrates the top k (= 5) classes of interest captured in a predefined learning window. The re-calibration process ensures that the tracking mechanism can dynamically adapt to the changing user inclinations. The second step (Line 4) extracts the intermediate feature map for the incoming batch of data 2 .

In the next step, we train the network parameters g ϕ with the complete short-term memory M s for each new data sample 3 . Furthermore, we periodically select a subset of elements (Line 5-6) from the long-term store M l and train the network with the selected data instances. Concurrently, we update the short-term memory (Line 10-12) using our proposed user-aware uncertainty-guided sampling method in the following step 4 . In the last and final step, we leverage latent feature maps stored in the short-term store to update long-term memory (Line 14-17) based on our class-prototypebased sampling scheme 5 . We explain our memory update and retrieval strategies in more detail next. The objective of the short-term memory is to mitigate catastrophic forgetting and build personalized models. For this purpose, we leverage two major characteristics of the incoming samples: user affinity and uncertainty. First, if the samples belong to different classes in the incoming batch, then

1) Condition 1: In particular, for user-centric sampling, we employ an allocation factor ∆ k based on the running statistics of the data instances as:

∆ k = n k ρ (n k + n N -k ) ρ (2

)

where N is the total number of encountered classes, k refers to the total number of classes of interest, ρ is a hyperparameter controlling the allocation factor, and n k is the average running frequency of classes of user-interest estimated during learning window l.

This criterion ∆ upscales the ratio of the average number of samples belonging to preferred classes w.r.t total class instances. For ρ = 0, all classes are equally favorable, and for ρ = 1, classes are assigned in proportion to their running frequencies. In our experiments, ρ is chosen between 0 and 1 such that the data acquisition favors the classes of user-interest and suppresses the interference caused by non-preferred class instances. We update the value of the allocation factor after each learning window (∼1500 images).

2) Condition 2: As we are learning in a streaming fashion, not all samples would equally affect the model performance. If some samples are more challenging to learn or previously unseen by the model, it is essential to store and rehearse the network with such instances to improve the overall robustness. Generally, samples that are closer to the decision boundary fall under this purview. However, directly computing decision boundaries for each sample is intractable and computationally expensive. Instead, we leverage logit-values, i.e., the final output response of the model as a measure of their pseudodistance from the decision boundary. To meet this objective, we assign a score U i for each element x i in the incoming mini-batch B t :

U i = N c=1 |o(x i ) c y c |(3)

where o(x i ) refers to the network logit scores for each element x i , y refers to the one-hot encoded output of the label y i and N refers to the total number of classes. A low logit score U i indicates that the network is uncertain about these samples and hence must be replayed again. In other words, samples with high U -1 i value should be retained. We define a discrete non-uniform probability distribution to jointly select an element from the incoming mini-batch B t based on the above two conditions and randomly replace it with a sample currently stored in the short-term store, where

p i ∝ α • ∆ i yi∈k ∆ k + yi∈N -k (1 -∆ k ) + β • U -1 i (4)

The weighted combination of ∆ k and U -1 i (via hyperparameters α and β) helps us cater to instances belonging to userinterest more effectively and handle their relative complexities in terms of model uncertainty. The goal of the long-term memory is to promote prolonged and effective retention and improve overall model generalizability. To maintain a well-rounded representation of the past and present incoming samples, preserving diverse and representative samples from the stream is vital. For this purpose, we introduce a class-balanced sampling technique storing an equal number of samples for each class in the longterm store. Inspired by [34], we propose to select contrastive samples based on their distance from the class prototypes in the latent space representation. We first define class prototypes for each class:

P c = 1 L c Lc l=1 Z l(5)

where Z l corresponds to the latent activation maps corresponding to class c currently stored in the long-term memory and L c is the total number of such class instances in the longterm memory. Here, the class prototypes roughly approximate the center of mass in the latent space.

We hypothesize that if any two samples belong to the same class (similarity) and their model predictions vary drastically (diversity), then such samples should be more informative about their respective class distribution in the latent space.

To select such samples, we formulate a computationally inexpensive measure using Kullback-Leibler divergence (KLdivergence) criteria to approximate the distance between a datapoint belonging to that class and the respective class prototype.

For each sample st j belonging to class c already stored in the short-term store, we calculate:

S j = tanh(KL(p(y|st j ) ∥ p(y|P c )))(6)

where p(y|st j )) refers to the softmax probabilities for each element st j and p(y|P c )) indicates the softmax probabilities for class-prototypes P c . A high S j score indicates that the data point disagrees in softmax probabilities against other points of the same class already present in the long-term store. Thus, we greedily select the sample with the maximum value of S j score and randomly replace it with other samples of the same class already present in the long-term memory.

Chameleon surpasses other methods in terms of accuracy while incurring minimal memory overhead, as discussed in results later. Given that Latent Replay and SLDA exhibit similar accuracy to Chameleon, we conduct an extensive investigation of these three methods concerning latency and energy consumption on real edge devices, including FPGA, GPU, and TPU. At the start of execution, the CPU host transfers the weights and inputs to the on-chip memory. The accelerator then processes each layer sequentially. In our execution model, only one layer is executed at a time, and more advanced parallel scheduling between layers is beyond the scope of this work. The accelerator employs the IFM and OFM buffers as ping-pong buffers to minimize off-chip data communication overhead. For Chameleon, the long-term store resides in offchip memory, while for Latent Replay, a single replay buffer occupies the off-chip memory. Similar to conventional model training, the replay process consists of three steps: Forward Pass (FP), Backward Pass (BP), and Weight Update (WU), as illustrated in Figure 8. During the FP and WU stages, the accelerator utilizes the shortterm store, which is pre-populated with the activation values for the latent layer. The accelerator writes back the activation values for the last few layers from the convolution engine to the off-chip memory for reuse during the WU stage. Later, the original weights are transmitted again to the accelerator's weight buffer, along with the loss data. The convolution engine performs Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) operations using the activation data stored in the short-term store and the computed loss values from the previous step.

The computation engines process the incoming loss value together with the weights and transfer the resulting loss data to the off-chip memory at the end of execution for all layers. Our FPGA implementation is limited to Chameleon and Latent Replay [14] only, as implementing SLDA [30] on FPGA poses significant challenges due to its complex processing requirements such as inverse matrix operation. The exported RTL is synthesized and implemented using Vivado 2021.2 and reaches 150 MHz clock frequency. By utilizing this model, we can make informed decisions regarding design objectives related to replay, such as the optimal number of replay elements and the selection of the latent layer, considering the hardware constraints. In BP stage, the transposed weights are loaded back from the off-chip memory to the weight buffer, however with the same dimensions as during the forward pass. Hence, the communication cost of loading inputs, weights and storing intermediate loss values can be stated the same as the data transfer cost during the forward pass, i.e., load BP i ifm = load FP i ifm , load BP i wght = load FP i wght , and store BP i ofm = store FP i ofm . In WU stage, activation data is transmitted to the IFM buffer leading to load WU i ifm = load FP i ifm while the loss values are loaded to the OFM buffer from the on-chip buffer, costing load WU i ofm = store FP i ofm . After accumulating gradients for the entire batch, weights are updated and transmitted back to the off-chip buffer costing store WU i wght = load FP i wght same as loading them during previous two stages.

For Short-Term store, there will be a one-time cost of populating the buffer with the desired number of replay elements at the start of the execution. For long-term store, there will be extra overhead for loading each new replay element from the off-chip memory.

Total loading latency for each stage will be governed by max{load FP i ifm , load FP i wei }. Consequently, total replay cost load total for loading inputs and weights for the entire model with the latent layer ℓ rep and total ℓ layers can be formulated as:

load total = rep≤i≤ℓ max{load FP i ifm , load FP i wght } + rep≤i≤ℓ max{load BP i ifm , load BP i wght } + rep≤i≤ℓ max{load WU i ifm , load WU i ofm }(19)

Similarly, total replay cost store total for storing the resultant output feature maps to the off-chip memory with total ℓ layers can be formulated as:

store total = rep≤i≤ℓ (store FP i ofm + store BP i ofm + store WU i wght )(20)

Finally, our objective is to minimize the cumulative cost of replay, considering both the computation and communication costs, while satisfying the constraints on BRAM memory consumption. The objective function L obj can be formulated as follows:

L obj = min{comp total + load total + store total }(21)

To evaluate the performance of our proposed algorithm, we conduct latency and energy measurements using an Edge TPU inspired template-based machine learning accelerator. The template design consists of a 2D array of processing elements (PEs) and on-chip staging buffers for storing model parameters, activations, and outputs. For our experiments, we employ the uSystolic-Sim [36] cycle-accurate simulator. We configure the simulator with a (64,64) PE array, 8 MB of on-chip memory, and a clock frequency of 400 MHz, which closely resembles the Edge TPU architecture. Since the Edge TPU supports only INT8 multiplication, we quantize the fixed part of our network to INT8. Following the approach outlined in [37], we utilized the BFP16 datatype for computing the forward and backward pass of the last few layers of the network on the device while offloading the gradient updates to the CPU. This hybrid precision scheme allows us to strike a balance between accuracy and computational efficiency.

subsection: C. Edge GPU based Continual learning
text: We conduct additional experiments using the PyTorch framework on an NVIDIA Jetson Nano to further evaluate the tradeoff between latency, energy, and accuracy. The Jetson Nano is a low-power, energy-efficient GPU device that features a 128-core integrated NVIDIA Maxwell GPU and a quadcore 64-bit ARM CPU. It is equipped with 4 GB of LPDDR4 memory and an additional 4GB of SWAP space. To emulate our framework on the Jetson Nano, we utilize the available RAM for the short-term store and the SWAP space for the long-term store. Since direct access to the on-chip L2 Cache on the GPU is not possible, we adapted our storage strategy accordingly. During the training process, we maintain a batch size of 8 to ensure reasonable training times while considering the resource constraints of the Jetson Nano. This batch size allows us to effectively evaluate the performance of different methods while accommodating the device's capabilities.

Dataset. For our evaluation, we consider the Domain Incremental Learning (Domain-IL) setting, where the input distribution undergoes a domain shift over time where each domain is characterized by distinct backgrounds and lighting, as shown in Figure 10. The task is to incrementally learn objects under different domains from the training set. Further, the task identities remain unknown for all our experiments. Existing works evaluate Domain-IL on Rotation MNIST [38] and Permutation MNIST [6]. However, they do not offer a very realistic CL setting since distributional shifts across tasks are abrupt, as previously criticized by [39]. To evaluate our experiments in realistic streaming learning setup, we rely on two robotics-based large-scale CL benchmarks CORe50 [3] and OpenLORIS-Object [40] datasets. Simulating user-aware data streams. To evaluate our method in user-aware incremental learning scenarios, we introduce three distinct frequency distributions for the CORe50 dataset, inspired by [41]. These distributions simulate varied user preferences and allow us to assess the adaptability of our approach under different class imbalances, as depicted in Figure 11. The three learning schemes are as follows:

• Learning Scheme 1 simulates a scenario where the model attends to a fixed number of classes over time, with diminishing interest in other classes. This scheme down-samples non-preferred class samples while keeping preferred class samples constant. • Learning Scheme 2 simulates a scenario where users initially explore various classes but gradually become biased towards certain classes. This scheme gradually upsamples user-preferred class instances while keeping non-preferred class instances constant. • Learning Scheme 3 combines the pattern of the second scheme with further suppression of non-preferred class samples, widening the gap between the two groups. This scheme simulates a decreasing geometric series for nonpreferred classes while using the same geometric series as in the second scheme for preferred classes. The utility factor balances the trade-off between class imbalances and representation. In the first learning scheme, the maximum imbalance between the two sets of classes is 10 to 1, with the number of user-preferred class samples remaining constant while gradually reducing non-preferred class samples. The ratio for the other two learning schemes is 2 to 1 and 4 to 1, respectively. Learning scheme 2 keeps the number of non-preferred class samples constant while gradually increasing the preferred ones. Learning scheme three gradually increases preferred class samples and reduces nonpreferred classes. We perform ten runs for each experiment and randomly sample 5 user-preferred classes in each run to investigate the effectiveness of our method against changing user preferences. We strictly compare all baseline methods on the same set of classes.

Base Models & Hyperparameters. Considering the limited computational resources available on the device, we pick a hardware-friendly CNN, MobileNetV1 [42], pre-trained on the ImageNet dataset for our base experiments. We also experiment with ResNet-18, VGG-16 and ShuffleNet to evaluate the generalizability of our method across different models. We use a small batch size of 10, and a learning rate of 0.001 with the SGD optimizer [2]. Each sample passes through the model only once. We update short-term memory for every incoming batch while long-term memory for every ten batches to maintain the on-chip/off-chip memory access trade-off. In each epoch, we concatenate the complete short-term store elements while selecting one single sample from the longterm store with the incoming batch of samples. We experiment with the last few layers as the latent layer to keep the training overhead minimal. The latent layer is the layer from which we extract feature maps to store in the replay buffer. Based on the overall model accuracy, we choose layer 21 (out of 27 layers) of the MobileNetV1 as the latent layer.

Metrics. Following [12], we report final model accuracy, Acc all averaged over all classes at the end of model training over all domains. Acc all helps us quantify the generalizability of the model. We report final model accuracy, Acc all averaged over all classes at the end of training the model on all domains.

Acc all helps us quantify the generalizability of the model while Acc pref measures the performance over user-specific class interests. Additionally, we quantify the memory overhead for each continual learning method. For the same number of replay samples, different methods correspond to different memory overhead as the size of the replay buffer. Further, we report latency and energy consumption on various edge devices to validate the efficacy of over methods on resourceconstrained devices.

Baselines. For lower-bound on the average model accuracy, we finetune the training part of the network with a single epoch over the entire dataset without any replay buffer. For upper-bound on the average model accuracy, the model is jointly trained in a traditional machine learning paradigm for 4 epochs. We compare Chameleon against several stateof-the-art CL methods. We include two regularization-based methods: EWC++ [20] and LwF [21]. We also compare our method against SLDA [30], and adapt it for our objectlevel classification task. Finally, we compare our method against four single replay buffer based methods: GSS [22], ER [11], DER [12], and Latent Replay [14] with varying replay buffer sizes: 100, 200, 500, and 1500 samples to evaluate the memory-efficiency and scalability of different methods. For our method, we keep the size of shortterm memory (M s ) constant at 10 samples while varying the size of long-term memory (M l ). For the implementation of EWC++, LwF, GSS, ER, and DER, we rely on the codebase available at https://github.com/RaptorMai/ online-continual-learning. Similarly, for SLDA and Latent Replay, we refer to their official GitHub repositories: https:// github.com/tyler-hayes/SLDA-Tutorial and https://github.com/ vlomonaco/ar1-pytorch, respectively.

Accuracy comparison with other baselines. Table II compares Chameleon with state-of-the-art CL methods across varying replay buffer sizes averaged across ten runs. The JOINT training method reflects the upper bound for the overall model accuracy over the entire dataset with four epochs, making it infeasible for edge devices. The finetuning method provides the lower bound for the model accuracy without any measures to counter catastrophic forgetting.

For Chameleon, we keep 10 samples in the short-term store (M s ) and vary the size of the long-term store (M l ). Chameleon achieves the best accuracy on both OpenLORIS and CORe50 datasets with very low memory requirements, demonstrating the effectiveness of our memory update and retrieval strategies. Specifically, the short-term store dynamically switches between different classes of interest after each learning window. At the same time, the long-term store maintains the most salient class instances from previous domains uniformly, ensuring better results over other baseline methods. With the increasing size of the long-term store, we observe marginal improvement in the model accuracy since the performance is already at par with the upper bound, even at a small buffer size.

Overall, all methods perform better on the OpenLORIS dataset than the CORe50 dataset, primarily due to more training samples and smoother transitions between consecutive domains in the OpenLORIS dataset. On both datasets, the dismal accuracy of EWC++ and LwF is primarily attributed to gradient explosion on previous domains, leading to catastrophic forgetting. Interestingly, SLDA achieves comparable average model accuracy with limited memory utilization.

For replay-based methods, GSS seems less effective due to the sub-optimal selection strategy on previous domains, despite having a much larger memory footprint. GSS stores gradient direction vectors for each element in the buffer, resulting in up to 10x more memory overhead for the same number of replay samples. Methods like ER and DER fail to perform under tight memory constraints (≤ 200 replay samples), as also shown in Figure 1. Both methods store original input images and output responses for each element in the buffer, incurring huge space overhead. In comparison, both Latent Replay and Chameleon store only intermediate activations in the replay buffer, leading to substantial memory savings. However, Chameleon demonstrates a much better trade-off, outperforming Latent Replay by up to ∼7-8% in accuracy, especially across smaller memory budgets. We further evaluate Chameleon, SLDA, and Latent Replay with their respective original memory buffer sizes over varying user-preferences.

Effectiveness over varying user-preferences. We evaluate Chameleon with two other resource-efficient methods, SLDA and Latent Replay, on three different learning schemes, which were described earlier with the major objective of maximizing the accuracy over user-preferred classes (Acc pref ). Table III provides a comprehensive comparison between Chameleon, Latent Replay, and SLDA. Chameleon achieves significant improvements over all baselines, resulting in a relative improvement of approximately 2% in average model accuracy (Acc all ) and approximately 5% in accuracy over preferred classes (Acc pref ) compared to SLDA. It is worth noting that Chameleon and SLDA achieve comparable average model accuracy while utilizing limited memory resources. However, Chameleon demonstrates a better trade-off by outperforming SLDA by approximately 7-8% in accuracy for user-

Performance over different latent layers. We compare the performance of the MobileNetv1 architecture across different latent layers, as shown in Table IV. All experiments utilize the 10 replay patterns in the short-term store and 100 replay patterns in the long-term store. From the results, we observed that as we progress towards the latter layers, the accuracy for user-preferred classes (Acc pref ) either remains constant or slightly decreases. However, the overall model accuracy is significantly affected. This indicates that the latter layers are more biased towards majority class samples. This observation aligns with the general understanding of CNNs, where initial layers capture class-generic features while the latter focus on class-specific features. Furthermore, we notice that layer 27 consumes up to 50% less memory per output feature map compared to layer 21. This limited layer capacity can impact its ability to be class-agnostic, consequently affecting the overall model accuracy. Nevertheless, this limitation can be addressed by increasing the number of replay elements in the replay buffer for the latter layers. Additionally, edge devices with specific requirements towards user-specific performance and minimal memory can choose to work with the feature maps of the last few layers to achieve satisfactory results. This trade-off allows for tailoring the model's capabilities to the device's available resources and user preferences. Evaluation with other models. To demonstrate Chameleon's generalizability, we evaluate memory overhead and model accuracy over preferred classes (Acc pref ) on diverse DNN models: ResNet-18 [43], ShuffleNet [44], and VGG-16 [45], as shown in Figure 13. We experiment with various layers as the latent layer for these networks and finally select layer 10, layer 11, and layer 18 as the latent layer for ResNet-18, VGG-16, and ShuffleNet, respectively, for both Latent Replay and Chameleon. These layers serve as the source for extracting feature maps to be stored in the replay buffer. For Chameleon, we maintain 10 samples in the short-term store and 100 samples in the long-term store, while for Latent Replay, we store 1500 samples in the replay buffer across all models. Chameleon achieves comparable or even better accuracy than Latent Replay while significantly reducing the memory overhead. In fact, Chameleon consumes about 15 times less memory than that of Latent Replay. This reduction in memory overhead is particularly notable in the case of VGG-16, where each replay element is four times the size of MobileNetV1. As a result, while Latent Replay consumes approximately 200 MB of memory for VGG-16, Chameleon requires less than 12 MB of total memory overhead (approximately 1 MB on-chip). Furthermore, Chameleon consistently outperforms the SLDA method by up to 10% accuracy across all the benchmark models.

Effectiveness of two sampling techniques. We analyze the impact of each replay buffer in Table V on learning scheme 3. The short-term memory buffer exhibits significant improvements in accuracy for preferred classes due to its useraware sampling policy. Conversely, the long-term memory store demonstrates good performance in terms of average model accuracy, benefiting from a balanced distribution of memory for all classes. Both buffers contribute to performance improvement, collaborating and individually, as their sampling strategies play a crucial role in achieving higher accuracy and balanced class representation. Chameleon effectively utilizes both buffers to enhance the learning process in a user-aware and balanced manner.

subsection: D. Hardware Efficiency of our proposed framework
text:
Latency and Energy on Edge FPGA. We focus on the MobileNetV1 architecture to validate the efficacy of our proposed framework. The MobileNetV1 architecture consists of depthwise and pointwise convolutions, which have different compute patterns compared to standard convolutions. This aspect dramatically influences our design choices, especially with respect to various tile sizes and the latent layer selection.

For the first four layers, we fixed the tile sizes [T n , T m , T r , T c ] as [16,16,8,8], modified them to [32,32,4,4] for the last three layers, and kept them as [32,32,8,8] for the rest of the layers. Figure 14 illustrates the estimated analytical cost of different latent layers for compute and data transfer using our performance model, as described in Section IV. As expected, the overall cost decreases as we approach the last layer in the model, with data transfer dominating the total execution time. Since the entire model is frozen below the selected latent layer, the communication cost for loading and storing the intermediate outputs for each compute phase (FP, BP, WU) significantly decreases as we choose the latter layers for replay. To further validate the effectiveness of our proposed analytical framework, we compared it against the actual on-device measurements for both Chameleon-Accel and Latent Replay on the AMD ZCU102 board, as shown in Figure 15. The data transfer cost closely follows the analytical model, while the compute cost diverges marginally due to the extra computation for non-linear functions. Overall, our method provides significant insights into the overall resource consumption and theoretical performance of the model. and ten replay elements per incoming input. Latent Replay spends a majority of the overall latency in data movement of latent activations, which is a significant factor impacting its performance. In contrast, Chameleon-Accel effectively leverages on-chip memory due to our proposed hierarchical buffer and sampling policies, leading to superior performance. Figure 16 shows the overall memory breakdown with various components, with latent activations significantly dominating the memory footprint in the case of Latent Replay.

In this work, we evaluate both methods on the same compute engine and achieve reasonable performance for a training accelerator with 16-bit floating-point operations. For instance, the state-of-the-art FPGA framework [46] takes 462ms for training SqueezeNetV1 [47], similar to the MobileNetV1 architecture on the Intel Stratix 10 board. More advanced hardware optimizations, such as reduced precision training on FPGAs, can further decrease the compute time and are left for future exploration.

Latency and Energy on EdgeTPU. We evaluate Chameleon-Accel and SLDA on a custom TPU-like edge accelerator. For SLDA, the method requires a matrix pseudoinverse to update the covariance matrix in the final output computation. We performed this step on the CPU since our accelerator only supports GEMM operation. We do not encounter any such difficulties with Chameleon since our approach can be trained in an end-to-end fashion. As shown in Table VI, our method achieves roughly 11.7 × speedup over SLDA in terms of execution time per input image. This is due to the O(N 3 ) complexity of matrix inverse operation, which cannot take full advantage of the GEMM accelerator.

Latency and Energy on Edge GPU. Table VI shows latency and energy per image for Chameleon-Accel, SLDA, and Latent Replay. We observe up to 2.1× and 3.5× speedup compared to SLDA and Latent Replay, respectively. Similar to Chameleon-Accel, SLDA also processes the input in a single pass; however, it still incurs huge latency and energy costs as it requires a pseudo-matrix inverse operation for each image. Similarly, Latent Replay suffers from high memory overhead. We note that all methods perform comparatively better on the GPU than our FPGA implementation because of batch processing and a highly efficient floating-point processing engine on the GPU. Also, while we could not take advantage of the on-chip L2 Cache on the GPU, our proposed framework still outperforms the other two baselines, establishing the effectiveness of our sample selection strategies.

We propose Chameleon, a resource-efficient personalized continual learning framework. Chameleon maintains decoupled replay buffers -short-term and long-term stores complementary to the on-chip and off-chip memory interface. We also introduce an FPGA-based cost-modeling framework to accurately estimate computation and data transfer costs for different latent layers and models, streamlining the task of understanding accuracy-hardware performance tradeoffs. Our evaluations show Chameleon accomplishes over 7 -8% better accuracy than other CL methods with 16× less memory, 6.75× less latency, and 7× less energy compared to the state-of-theart methods.
